title: About Three Feet
author: Jo Lein
summary: Jo Lein reflects on moving from sixteen years of leveraged, indirect influence on education, coaching teachers, leaders and systems, back to a middle school where she handles attendance, discipline and hallways and knows students by name again. She admits the move unsettles her professional identity as a coach and exposes a suspicion that she gravitates toward work that gives immediate, gratifying feedback from kids rather than the slower payoff of fixing systems. Attendance becomes her test case, since it needs tiers, data and case management, yet a six-second 'glad you're here' to one returning student matters just as much. She concludes that the answer is both levels at once and that she no longer believes in a tidy percentage-based balance of leadership time. The piece ends by questioning whether a five-minute conversation needs a multiplier to be worthwhile.
points: Education careers reward moving away from students to gain leverage, but that distance can quietly erode a leader's actual knowledge of the kids the system exists to serve.

Immediate feedback from children can tempt a school leader to choose the work that feels useful over the systems work that is more valuable but less rewarding, and honest self-suspicion about this is a healthy check.
Attendance illustrates that school improvement is a both-and: a sophisticated system fails if no one is glad students came, and a warm welcome fails without a system behind it.
The author rejects fixed time ratios for leadership priorities because schools and humans do not work that way, and the right move shifts from day to day.
A short conversation with one student may have no multiplier effect and can still be enough on its own terms.
quotes: Sixteen years ago, my influence was incredibly small…a single classroom, with my students, my instruction, and my relationships.
Eventually those skills became something more dangerous than expertise…an IDENTITY. I was a coach.
I don’t want to tell myself a heroic story about relationships when the truth might sometimes be that I choose the work that makes me feel immediately useful.
Nobody yells your name excitedly because you improved the attendance workflow. The spreadsheet has never once complimented my outfit or my amazingly coordinated earrings and shoes.

If I spend my entire day saying “glad you’re here,” I have failed to build an attendance system. If I build the world’s most sophisticated attendance system and kids can walk through our doors without anyone being glad they’re here, I think I have failed too.
I don’t think I believe in balance anymore. Balance suggests there is some correct distribution of minutes that I could discover if I were just disciplined enough.
Maybe this five-minute conversation won’t increase attendance. Maybe it won’t prevent the next conflict.
Some of my favorite moments now travel about three feet. Maybe that’s enough.
